flashcard_questions.q: Which battle inspired Tennyson's ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’?
flashcard_questions.a: The Battle of Balaclava, during the Crimean War.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Tennyson write ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’?
What effect does the repeated “Half a league” opening create?
flashcard_questions.a: A galloping rhythm that mimics the horses' hooves and the unstoppable momentum of the charge.

flashcard_questions.q: Which biblical metaphor names the place the soldiers ride into?
flashcard_questions.a: “the valley of Death”, an echo of Psalm 23.

flashcard_questions.q: Which three rhyming lines sum up the soldiers' unquestioning obedience?
flashcard_questions.a: “Theirs not to make reply, / Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die”

flashcard_questions.q: Which phrase admits that the order to charge was a mistake?
What does the personification in “Into the jaws of Death” suggest?
flashcard_questions.a: The battlefield is a monster that devours the soldiers.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the shift from “Rode the six hundred” to “Left of six hundred” track?
Which metre in Tennyson's poem mimics the rhythm of galloping horses?
Whose experiences did Hughes draw on when writing ‘Bayonet Charge’?
flashcard_questions.a: His father's, who fought in the First World War.

flashcard_questions.q: Which opening line throws the reader straight into the action of ‘Bayonet Charge’?
flashcard_questions.a: “Suddenly he awoke and was running — raw”

flashcard_questions.q: What does the personification in “Bullets smacking the belly out of the air” suggest?
flashcard_questions.a: The bullets are ripping through the very atmosphere around the soldier.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the metaphor “cold clockwork of the stars and the nations” present war as?
flashcard_questions.a: A mechanical, unfeeling machine in which individual soldiers are only cogs.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the yellow hare symbolise in ‘Bayonet Charge’?
flashcard_questions.a: The destruction of innocence in war.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the simile “Dropped like luxuries” suggest about patriotic ideals?
flashcard_questions.a: In terror, noble ideas are the first things a soldier abandons.

notes: 15 cards: 6 quotation-to-technique or effect, 4 theme-to-quotation, 2 structure and form (dactylic metre, the shifting refrain), 2 context-to-relevance (Balaclava, Hughes's father), 1 date card. Dropped metaphor, personification, patriotic and patriotism as definition cards — all four are tested through named examples in the poems, and 'patriotic' and 'patriotism' would interfere with each other.
